items.subject: index_patient

evidence.quote: Patient 1 presented at 3 months of age with severe, exudative eczema unresponsive to emollients, 1% hydrocortisone and fusidic acid. She was exclusively breastfed, with longstanding reflux and vomiting after feeds, for which her mother had excluded cow’s milk from her diet. The patient was referred to allergy, dietetics, and dermatology services, and her treatment was escalated to include Fucidin H and topical tacrolimus. On review at 9 months of age, there was some improvement in eczema control, but she remained predominantly breastfed with severe aversive feeding, despite thickeners and exclusion of allergens from her mother’s diet after skin prick testing. Her weight dropped below the 0.4th centile, and blood tests showed marked deficiencies of iron, vitamin D and sodium with severe hyperkalemia. Due to the acute electrolyte imbalance and failure to thrive, she was admitted for supplementation and nasogastric feeding. During her admission, the initial hyponatremia (129 mmol/L) and hyperkalemia (7.4 mmol/L) improved (Table 1), normalizing a few days after discharge. Her renal function and renal ultrasound were normal throughout with low urinary sodium concentration (8 mmol/L). A

urinary steroid profile requested while she was hyponatremic showed features of PHA, with increases of aldosterone precursors, corticosterone and aldosterone metabolites, excluding all saltwasting forms of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) and aldosterone synthase deficiency. Further endocrine investigations were performed 2 months after discharge showing normal sodium and potassium levels with borderline high aldosterone level of 6,750 pmol/L (indicative age-related range <1,000 pmol/L), normal renin activity and improvement in eczema control (Table 1). At 20 months of age, her aldosterone had normalized, with no aversive eating symptoms, eczema flares occurring less than monthly and her weight tracking the 50th centile (Table 2).

Patient 1 presented at 3 months of age with severe, exudative eczema unresponsive to emollients, 1% hydrocortisone and fusidic acid. She was exclusively breastfed, with longstanding reflux and vomiting after feeds, for which her mother had excluded cow’s milk from her diet. The patient was referred to allergy, dietetics, and dermatology services, and her treatment was escalated to include Fucidin H and topical tacrolimus. On review at 9 months of age, there was some improvement in eczema control, but she remained predominantly breastfed with severe aversive feeding, despite thickeners and exclusion of allergens from her mother’s diet after skin prick testing. Her weight dropped below the 0.4th centile, and blood tests showed marked deficiencies of iron, vitamin D and sodium with severe hyperkalemia. Due to the acute electrolyte imbalance and failure to thrive, she was admitted for supplementation and nasogastric feeding. During her admission, the initial hyponatremia (129 mmol/L) and hyperkalemia (7.4 mmol/L) improved (Table 1), normalizing a few days after discharge. Her renal function and renal ultrasound were normal throughout with low urinary sodium concentration (8 mmol/L). A urinary steroid profile requested while she was hyponatremic showed features of PHA, with increases of aldosterone precursors, corticosterone and aldosterone metabolites, excluding all saltwasting forms of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) and aldosterone synthase deficiency. Further endocrine investigations were performed 2 months after discharge showing normal sodium and potassium levels with borderline high aldosterone level of 6,750 pmol/L (indicative age-related range <1,000 pmol/L), normal renin activity and improvement in eczema control (Table 1). At 20 months of age, her aldosterone had normalized, with no aversive eating symptoms, eczema flares occurring less than monthly and her weight tracking the 50th centile (Table 2).

evidence.quote: Patient 1 presented at 3 months of age with severe, exudative eczema unresponsive to emollients, 1% hydrocortisone and fusidic acid. She was exclusively breastfed, with longstanding reflux and vomiting after feeds, for which her mother had excluded cow’s milk from her diet. The patient was referred to allergy, dietetics, and dermatology services, and her treatment was escalated to include Fucidin H and topical tacrolimus. On review at 9 months of age, there was some improvement in eczema control, but she remained predominantly breastfed with severe aversive feeding, despite thickeners and exclusion of allergens from her mother’s diet after skin prick testing. Her weight dropped below the 0.4th centile, and blood tests showed marked deficiencies of iron, vitamin D and sodium with severe hyperkalemia. Due to the acute electrolyte imbalance and failure to thrive, she was admitted for supplementation and nasogastric feeding. During her admission, the initial hyponatremia (129 mmol/L) and hyperkalemia (7.4 mmol/L) improved (Table 1), normalizing a few days after discharge. Her renal function and renal ultrasound were normal throughout with low urinary sodium concentration (8 mmol/L). A

urinary steroid profile requested while she was hyponatremic showed features of PHA, with increases of aldosterone precursors, corticosterone and aldosterone metabolites, excluding all saltwasting forms of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) and aldosterone synthase deficiency. Further endocrine investigations were performed 2 months after discharge showing normal sodium and potassium levels with borderline high aldosterone level of 6,750 pmol/L (indicative age-related range <1,000 pmol/L), normal renin activity and improvement in eczema control (Table 1). At 20 months of age, her aldosterone had normalized, with no aversive eating symptoms, eczema flares occurring less than monthly and her weight tracking the 50th centile (Table 2).

Patient 2 presented at 7 months with 24 hours of lethargy and vomiting after feeds. His eczema had been managed with emollients, 1% hydrocortisone and fusidic acid, and now appeared to be infected and exudative. Formula had recently been added to his diet, after 6 months of exclusive breastfeeding, with his mother following a vegan diet. His weight was below the 0.4th centile (21st at birth). Initial blood tests showed marked hyponatremia of 115 mmol/L and hyperkalemia of 6.4 mmol/L with normal renal function (Table 1). This was associated with aldosterone levels >40,000 pmol/L (indicative age-related range < 2,000 pmol/L) and an elevated plasma renin activity of 22.4 nmol/L/h (indicative agerelated range <11 nmol/L/hr). An elevated white blood cell count of 40.6×109/L (lymphocytes 17.9×109/L, eosinophils 13×109/L, no blasts) and thrombocytosis were also noted. Patient 2 was admitted for intravenous fluids given his hyponatremia and IV flucloxacillin for infected eczema. Dermatology optimized his steroid regimen, and an amino acid formula was started due to concerns regarding cow’s milk protein allergy (CMPA). He was discussed with endocrinology and discharged with a sodium of 131

mmol/L (sodium level at the point of discharge from admission). On review at 11 months, his eczema and weight had improved (Table 2) – skin prick testing showed sensitization to milk, nuts, lentils and coconut, and so continued exclusion of these foods was recommended. Repeat bloods showed complete resolution of the electrolyte disturbances and normalization of aldosterone and renin levels.

Formula had recently been added to his diet, after 6 months of exclusive breastfeeding, with his mother following a vegan diet. His weight was below the 0.4th centile (21st at birth). Initial blood tests showed marked hyponatremia of 115 mmol/L and hyperkalemia of 6.4 mmol/L with normal renal function (Table 1). This was associated with aldosterone levels >40,000 pmol/L (indicative age-related range < 2,000 pmol/L) and an elevated plasma renin activity of 22.4 nmol/L/h (indicative agerelated range <11 nmol/L/hr). An elevated white blood cell count of 40.6×109/L (lymphocytes 17.9×109/L, eosinophils 13×109/L, no blasts) and thrombocytosis were also noted. Patient 2 was admitted for intravenous fluids given his hyponatremia and IV flucloxacillin for infected eczema. Dermatology optimized his steroid regimen, and an amino acid formula was started due to concerns regarding cow’s milk protein allergy (CMPA). He was discussed with endocrinology and discharged with a sodium of 131 mmol/L (sodium level at the point of discharge from admission). On review at 11 months, his eczema and weight had improved (Table 2) – skin prick testing showed sensitization to milk, nuts, lentils and coconut, and so continued exclusion of these foods was recommended. Repeat bloods showed complete resolution of the electrolyte disturbances and normalization of aldosterone and renin levels.

events.description: Earlier eczema therapy and exclusive breastfeeding followed by recent formula; maternal vegan diet

evidence.quote: Patient 2 presented at 7 months with 24 hours of lethargy and vomiting after feeds. His eczema had been managed with emollients, 1% hydrocortisone and fusidic acid, and now appeared to be infected and exudative. Formula had recently been added to his diet, after 6 months of exclusive breastfeeding, with his mother following a vegan diet. His weight was below the 0.4th centile (21st at birth). Initial blood tests showed marked hyponatremia of 115 mmol/L and hyperkalemia of 6.4 mmol/L with normal renal function (Table 1). This was associated with aldosterone levels >40,000 pmol/L (indicative age-related range < 2,000 pmol/L) and an elevated plasma renin activity of 22.4 nmol/L/h (indicative agerelated range <11 nmol/L/hr). An elevated white blood cell count of 40.6×109/L (lymphocytes 17.9×109/L, eosinophils 13×109/L, no blasts) and thrombocytosis were also noted. Patient 2 was admitted for intravenous fluids given his hyponatremia and IV flucloxacillin for infected eczema. Dermatology optimized his steroid regimen, and an amino acid formula was started due to concerns regarding cow’s milk protein allergy (CMPA). He was discussed with endocrinology and discharged with a sodium of 131 mmol/L (sodium level at the point of discharge from admission). On review at 11 months, his eczema and weight had improved (Table 2) – skin prick testing showed sensitization to milk, nuts, lentils and coconut, and so continued exclusion of these foods was recommended. Repeat bloods showed complete resolution of the electrolyte disturbances and normalization of aldosterone and renin levels.

Patient 2 presented at 7 months with 24 hours of lethargy and vomiting after feeds. His eczema had been managed with emollients, 1% hydrocortisone and fusidic acid, and now appeared to be infected and exudative. Formula had recently been added to his diet, after 6 months of exclusive breastfeeding, with his mother following a vegan diet. His weight was below the 0.4th centile (21st at birth). Initial blood tests showed marked hyponatremia of 115 mmol/L and hyperkalemia of 6.4 mmol/L with normal renal function (Table 1). This was associated with aldosterone levels >40,000 pmol/L (indicative age-related range < 2,000 pmol/L) and an elevated plasma renin activity of 22.4 nmol/L/h (indicative agerelated range <11 nmol/L/hr). An elevated white blood cell count of 40.6×109/L (lymphocytes 17.9×109/L, eosinophils 13×109/L, no blasts) and thrombocytosis were also noted. Patient 2 was admitted for intravenous fluids given his hyponatremia and IV flucloxacillin for infected eczema. Dermatology optimized his steroid regimen, and an amino acid formula was started due to concerns regarding cow’s milk protein allergy (CMPA). He was discussed with endocrinology and discharged with a sodium of 131

mmol/L (sodium level at the point of discharge from admission). On review at 11 months, his eczema and weight had improved (Table 2) – skin prick testing showed sensitization to milk, nuts, lentils and coconut, and so continued exclusion of these foods was recommended. Repeat bloods showed complete resolution of the electrolyte disturbances and normalization of aldosterone and renin levels.

Patient 3 was reviewed at 5 months of age with a week of cough, vomiting, lethargy and severe exudative eczema. This had worsened over the last 2 months despite emollients, 1% hydrocortisone and maternal dairy and soya exclusion. He was admitted for IV antibiotics and started on potent topical steroids by dermatology. His laboratory results initially showed a metabolic acidosis with hyponatremia (sodium 121 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (potassium 6.3 mmol/L), with normal renal function including ultrasound and marked leukocytosis without blasts – white cell count 49.2 (lymphocytes 18.2×109/L, eosinophils 19.7×109/L). A urine sample taken in the Emergency Department (ED) showed low sodium excretion and urinary steroid profiling "consistent with PHA and excluding all salt-wasting forms of CAH and aldosterone synthase deficiency" (increased corticosterone and aldosterone metabolites – Table 1). He was initially treated in ED with a fluid bolus and initiation of maintenance fluids and sodium supplementation of 3 mmol/kg/day. Once on the ward, further investigations were performed showing mildly raised aldosterone levels at 3,360 pmol/L (indicative age-related range <2,000 pmol/L) and elevated

renin levels of 88.3 nmol/L/hr (indicative age-related range <11 nmol/L/hr). He was started on an amino acid formula to complement breastfeeding for suspected CMPA – skin prick testing confirmed sensitization to milk, nuts and house dust mites, with concerns of delayed soya allergy, so his mother continued to exclude these. At 3 months postdischarge, his eczema had improved considerably and renin levels had normalized.

Patient 3 was reviewed at 5 months of age with a week of cough, vomiting, lethargy and severe exudative eczema. This had worsened over the last 2 months despite emollients, 1% hydrocortisone and maternal dairy and soya exclusion. He was admitted for IV antibiotics and started on potent topical steroids by dermatology. His laboratory results initially showed a metabolic acidosis with hyponatremia (sodium 121 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (potassium 6.3 mmol/L), with normal renal function including ultrasound and marked leukocytosis without blasts – white cell count 49.2 (lymphocytes 18.2×109/L, eosinophils 19.7×109/L). A urine sample taken in the Emergency Department (ED) showed low sodium excretion and urinary steroid profiling "consistent with PHA and excluding all salt-wasting forms of CAH and aldosterone synthase deficiency" (increased corticosterone and aldosterone metabolites – Table 1). Once on the ward, further investigations were performed showing mildly raised aldosterone levels at 3,360 pmol/L (indicative age-related range <2,000 pmol/L) and elevated renin levels of 88.3 nmol/L/hr (indicative age-related range <11 nmol/L/hr). He was started on an amino acid formula to complement breastfeeding for suspected CMPA – skin prick testing confirmed sensitization to milk, nuts and house dust mites, with concerns of delayed soya allergy, so his mother continued to exclude these. At 3 months postdischarge, his eczema had improved considerably and renin
levels had normalized.

events.description: Worsening eczema despite topical care and maternal dairy/soya exclusion

evidence.quote: Patient 3 was reviewed at 5 months of age with a week of cough, vomiting, lethargy and severe exudative eczema. This had worsened over the last 2 months despite emollients, 1% hydrocortisone and maternal dairy and soya exclusion. He was admitted for IV antibiotics and started on potent topical steroids by dermatology. His laboratory results initially showed a metabolic acidosis with hyponatremia (sodium 121 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (potassium 6.3 mmol/L), with normal renal function including ultrasound and marked leukocytosis without blasts – white cell count 49.2 (lymphocytes 18.2×109/L, eosinophils 19.7×109/L). A urine sample taken in the Emergency Department (ED) showed low sodium excretion and urinary steroid profiling "consistent with PHA and excluding all salt-wasting forms of CAH and aldosterone synthase deficiency" (increased corticosterone and aldosterone metabolites – Table 1). He was initially treated in ED with a fluid bolus and initiation of maintenance fluids and sodium supplementation of 3 mmol/kg/day. Once on the ward, further investigations were performed showing mildly raised aldosterone levels at 3,360 pmol/L (indicative age-related range <2,000 pmol/L) and elevated renin levels of 88.3 nmol/L/hr (indicative age-related range <11 nmol/L/hr). He was started on an amino acid formula to complement breastfeeding for suspected CMPA – skin prick testing confirmed sensitization to milk, nuts and house dust mites, with concerns of delayed soya allergy, so his mother continued to exclude these. At 3 months postdischarge, his eczema had improved considerably and renin levels had normalized.

Patient 3 was reviewed at 5 months of age with a week of cough, vomiting, lethargy and severe exudative eczema. This had worsened over the last 2 months despite emollients, 1% hydrocortisone and maternal dairy and soya exclusion. He was admitted for IV antibiotics and started on potent topical steroids by dermatology. His laboratory results initially showed a metabolic acidosis with hyponatremia (sodium 121 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (potassium 6.3 mmol/L), with normal renal function including ultrasound and marked leukocytosis without blasts – white cell count 49.2 (lymphocytes 18.2×109/L, eosinophils 19.7×109/L). A urine sample taken in the Emergency Department (ED) showed low sodium excretion and urinary steroid profiling "consistent with PHA and excluding all salt-wasting forms of CAH and aldosterone synthase deficiency" (increased corticosterone and aldosterone metabolites – Table 1). He was initially treated in ED with a fluid bolus and initiation of maintenance fluids and sodium supplementation of 3 mmol/kg/day. Once on the ward, further investigations were performed showing mildly raised aldosterone levels at 3,360 pmol/L (indicative age-related range <2,000 pmol/L) and elevated

renin levels of 88.3 nmol/L/hr (indicative age-related range <11 nmol/L/hr). He was started on an amino acid formula to complement breastfeeding for suspected CMPA – skin prick testing confirmed sensitization to milk, nuts and house dust mites, with concerns of delayed soya allergy, so his mother continued to exclude these. At 3 months postdischarge, his eczema had improved considerably and renin levels had normalized.
